pass_b_english: We are to be clothed with a heavenly dwelling, which is to say, immortality. This is what we groan for, not a laying aside of our present bodies, but rather to be clothed with immortality over them. We pray for the heavenly dwelling, and if we put it on, we will not be found naked. It is true that a corruptible body weighs down the soul (1 Corinthians 15:53), and this is why we groan, because we are weighed down by corruption. We yearn for the heavenly dwelling, for immortality to be put on over our present bodies.

The phrase 'to put on' indicates that we will be clothed with immortality over our present bodies. We groan because we are still in our corruptible bodies, but if we put on immortality, we will not be naked. The 'if indeed' is not an expression of doubt, but rather an affirmation and proof that the heavenly dwelling, when put on over our previously existing bodies, will not leave us naked. This is something that will happen when we have put on immortality, and we will not be persuaded to lay aside our first bodies, nor will we be naked of them. The mortal is swallowed up by life, not being destroyed, but rather being transformed into immortality. This is how it has been from the beginning, for it is written that God took dust from the earth and formed man (Genesis 2:7).

The perishable nature of humanity is destined to be overcome by the power of life, for it is written that God breathed into the face of man the breath of life (Genesis 2:7), and he became a living soul. However, sin has intervened, and death has been inserted between, as the apostle Paul so eloquently expresses. Nevertheless, God has been pleased to sum up all things in Christ, and through the Spirit, he has come to renew us to our original state.

As a guarantee of the imperishability that will be given to us in the later times of the age, the life-giving Spirit deposited by Christ is a pledge of our future resurrection. Now, we experience this Spirit as a firstfruits, but after the resurrection from the dead, we will experience it as a full measure. Then, when all corruption is destroyed, we will leap and say, beating against corruption, 'Where is your victory, O death, where is your sting, O Hades?' (1 Corinthians 15:55), for sin and death will cease, and Christ will reign over the saints in imperishability.

Those who possess the pledge of the Spirit and are rich in the hope of resurrection have a profound understanding, as if the expected things are already present. They claim that from now on, they do not know anyone according to human standards, for they have transcended the limitations of the flesh and are now spiritual beings, no longer bound by corruptible flesh. In this context, corruption refers to the weakness and decay of the human body.

The transformation towards the Life-Giving Word is a profound experience, one that liberates us from the bonds of death and sin. When righteousness in Christ is revealed, corruption is shaken off, and we are no longer confined to weak and fragile human flesh. The apostle's statement that he no longer knows Christ according to human standards is a testament to the profound nature of this transformation.
